claim: Prostate cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in men worldwide.
source: Prostate cancer (PrCa) is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in men worldwide and is responsible for the highest incidence of male cancer in the United States (Ferlay et al., 2015; Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferlay et al., 2015 and Siegel et al., 2019

claim: Prostate cancer is responsible for the highest incidence of male cancer in the United States.
source: Prostate cancer (PrCa) is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in men worldwide and is responsible for the highest incidence of male cancer in the United States (Ferlay et al., 2015; Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferlay et al., 2015 and Siegel et al., 2019

claim: HOXB13 exhibits germline mutation in a subset of familial prostate cancer.
source: One novel pathway to understand tumor etiology and disease progression as well as develop new treatments is through HOXB13, which exhibits germline mutation in a subset of familial PrCa.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: HOXB13 is the predominant HOX factor that drives development and differentiation of prostate epithelial cells.
source: HOXB13 is the predominant HOX factor that drives development and differentiation of prostate epithelial cells (Brechka et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brechka et al., 2017

claim: Germline mutations of HOXB13 confer a substantial risk of prostate cancer.
source: Germline mutations of HOXB13 confer a substantial risk of PrCa, but mutation frequency is rare within the general population (Brechka et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brechka et al., 2017

claim: Prostate tumors frequently harbor downregulation of MEIS1 and MEIS2.
source: On the other hand, our prior studies show that prostate tumors frequently harbor downregulation of the transcription factors and HOX binding partners MEIS1 and MEIS2 (myeloid ecotropic viral integration site 1/2) (Bhanvadia et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies by the authors (Bhanvadia et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2012)

claim: MEIS proteins function as critical transcriptional co-factors to bind HOX proteins and specify HOX gene targeting.
source: MEIS proteins function as critical transcriptional co-factors during development and within adult tissues to bind HOX proteins and specify HOX gene targeting (Merabet and Mann, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Merabet and Mann, 2016

claim: Most prostate cancer HOXB13 mutations are located within the MEIS-interacting domain.
source: Most PrCa HOXB13 mutations (including the original G84E mutation) are located within the MEIS-interacting domain, emphasizing the importance of MEIS/HOX interactions in prostate tumor biology.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Increased mRNA expression of MEIS1 and MEIS2 in prostate cancer is correlated with significantly longer overall survival in watchful waiting patients with mid-range Gleason scores.
source: We originally demonstrated that increased mRNA expression of MEIS1 and MEIS2 in PrCa is correlated with significantly longer overall survival in a large cohort of watchful waiting patients with mid-range Gleason scores (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors (Chen et al., 2012)

claim: Patients harboring MEIS-positive tumors have a significantly favorable outcome.
source: More recently, we and others demonstrated that patients harboring MEIS-positive tumors have a significantly favorable outcome; there is a step-wise decrease in both MEIS1 and MEIS2 expression as tumors progress to metastatic (Bhanvadia et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Nørgaard et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhanvadia et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Nørgaard et al., 2019

claim: There is a step-wise decrease in both MEIS1 and MEIS2 expression as tumors progress to metastatic.
source: More recently, we and others demonstrated that patients harboring MEIS-positive tumors have a significantly favorable outcome; there is a step-wise decrease in both MEIS1 and MEIS2 expression as tumors progress to metastatic (Bhanvadia et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Nørgaard et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhanvadia et al., 2018; Jeong et al., 2017; Nørgaard et al., 2019

claim: MEIS1 and MEIS2 mRNA expression is significantly decreased in prostate cancer cell lines compared to primary prostate epithelial cells.
source: Analysis of MEIS1 and MEIS2 expression in a panel of PrCa cell lines compared to primary prostate epithelial cell (PrEC) cultures revealed significantly decreased MEIS1 and MEIS2 mRNA (p<0.05, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Western blot analysis in all prostate cancer cell lines documented low protein levels of MEIS1 with the exception of androgen-receptor negative lines Du145 and PC3.
source: Similarly, western blot analysis in all PrCa cell lines documented low protein levels of MEIS1—with the exception of androgen-receptor (AR)-negative lines Du145 and PC3—as well as low levels of MEIS2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Depletion of both MEIS1 and MEIS2 in LAPC4 cells was necessary to promote tumor xenograft growth.
source: We previously demonstrated that depletion of both MEIS1 and MEIS2 in LAPC4 cells was necessary to promote tumor xenograft growth (Bhanvadia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors (Bhanvadia et al., 2018)

claim: Ectopic expression of either MEIS2A or MEIS2D isoforms are sufficient to inhibit cell growth.
source: Further, ectopic expression of either MEIS2A or MEIS2D isoforms are sufficient to inhibit cell growth, while expression of MEIS2E did not impact cell growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by cell growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: Expression of MEIS2E did not impact cell growth.
source: Further, ectopic expression of either MEIS2A or MEIS2D isoforms are sufficient to inhibit cell growth, while expression of MEIS2E did not impact cell growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by cell growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: The necessity of MEIS DNA binding to suppress cell growth is supported by the lack of growth suppression by MEIS2E.
source: These data support the necessity of MEIS DNA binding to suppress cell growth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MEIS2E, which lacks a DNA-binding homeodomain, does not suppress growth

claim: Decreased cell number over time with either MEIS1 or MEIS2A was not associated with increased cell death.
source: Decreased cell number over time with either MEIS1 or MEIS2A was not associated with increased cell death but was associated with significant accumulation of cells in the G1 phase and fewer cells in G2 (p<0.05, Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Decreased cell number over time with either MEIS1 or MEIS2A was associated with significant accumulation of cells in the G1 phase and fewer cells in G2.
source: Decreased cell number over time with either MEIS1 or MEIS2A was not associated with increased cell death but was associated with significant accumulation of cells in the G1 phase and fewer cells in G2 (p<0.05, Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Subcutaneous xenografting of CWR22Rv1 cells with exogenous MEIS expression into nude mice resulted in MEIS-mediated tumor suppression in vivo.
source: Subcutaneous xenografting of CWR22Rv1 cells with exogenous MEIS expression into nude mice also resulted in MEIS-mediated tumor suppression in vivo (p<0.05, Figure 1F&G).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1F&G with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: MEIS1-expressing cells showed significantly decreased migration in vitro compared to control cells.
source: MEIS1-expressing cells showed significantly decreased migration in vitro compared to control cells (p<0.05, Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 1H,I with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: MEIS1 and full-length MEIS2 are sufficient to slow prostate cancer cell proliferation and tumor growth via reduced G1/S phase transition and decreased migratory capacity.
source: Thus, both MEIS1 and full-length MEIS2 are sufficient to slow PrCa cell proliferation and tumor growth via reduced G1/S phase transition and decreased migratory capacity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including proliferation, cell cycle, and migration assays

claim: HOXB13 is the highest-expressed HOX gene across benign epithelium, tumor, and metastatic tissue in adult human prostate.
source: Comparative analyses of HOX gene mRNA expression using publicly-available RNA-Seq datasets of adult human prostate tissues demonstrated that HOXB13 is the highest-expressed (Pflueger et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2015) HOX gene across benign epithelium, tumor, and metastatic tissue; HOXA10 is the next-highest (FPKMs HOXB13 vs. HOXA10: benign, 167.69 vs 38.53; primary tumor, 197.40 vs 35.63; metastasis, 149.44 vs 28.03, Figure 2A; Bhanvadia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A with citations to Pflueger et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2015; Bhanvadia et al., 2018

claim: HOXA10 is the next-highest expressed HOX gene after HOXB13 in adult human prostate.
source: Comparative analyses of HOX gene mRNA expression using publicly-available RNA-Seq datasets of adult human prostate tissues demonstrated that HOXB13 is the highest-expressed (Pflueger et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2015) HOX gene across benign epithelium, tumor, and metastatic tissue; HOXA10 is the next-highest (FPKMs HOXB13 vs. HOXA10: benign, 167.69 vs 38.53; primary tumor, 197.40 vs 35.63; metastasis, 149.44 vs 28.03, Figure 2A; Bhanvadia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A with FPKM values

claim: HOX11–13 paralogs, including HOXB13, prefer to heterodimerize with MEIS1 and exclude PBX proteins.
source: Notably, HOX11–13 paralogs, including HOXB13, prefer to heterodimerize with MEIS1 (Shen et al., 1997a) and exclude PBX proteins (Shen et al., 1997b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 1997a and Shen et al., 1997b

claim: Interactions between MEIS1 and HOXB13 were detectable in normal prostate epithelial cells.
source: Interactions between MEIS1 and HOXB13 were detectable in normal PrECs; such interactions decreased with lower MEIS expression in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: MEIS1-HOXB13 interactions decreased with lower MEIS expression in prostate cancer cells.
source: Interactions between MEIS1 and HOXB13 were detectable in normal PrECs; such interactions decreased with lower MEIS expression in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: Ectopic MEIS1 expression in CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 prostate cancer cells was associated with increased MEIS-HOXB13 interactions compared to control cells.
source: Importantly, ectopic MEIS1 expression leading to growth suppression in CWR22Rv1- and LAPC4 PrCa cells was associated with increased MEIS-HOXB13 interactions compared to the respective cell line controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay quantification shown in Figure 2C

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of MEIS1 with HOXB13 was observed in primary prostate epithelial cells.
source: Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation of MEIS1 with HOXB13 was observed in PrECs, and increased MEIS1 pulldown was observed in CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cells ectopically expressing MEIS1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Increased MEIS1 pulldown was observed in CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cells ectopically expressing MEIS1.
source: Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation of MEIS1 with HOXB13 was observed in PrECs, and increased MEIS1 pulldown was observed in CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cells ectopically expressing MEIS1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Loss of normal MEIS-HOXB13 interactions by decreased MEIS expression could enable non-canonical HOXB13 binding partners to partner with HOXB13 to promote oncogenesis and tumor progression.
source: These data also suggest that loss of normal MEIS-HOXB13 interactions by decreased MEIS expression could enable non-canonical HOXB13 binding partners to partner with HOXB13 to promote oncogenesis and tumor progression.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data

claim: In CWR22Rv1 cells, neither HOXB13 knockout alone nor HOXB13 knockout with MEIS1 expression significantly differed from control cells in proliferation.
source: In CWR22Rv1 cells, neither HOXB13ko alone nor HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 lines significantly differed from control cells, while LV-MEIS1 (with HOXB13 present) remained growth-suppressed (p<0.05, Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3B

claim: In CWR22Rv1 cells, LV-MEIS1 with HOXB13 present remained growth-suppressed.
source: In CWR22Rv1 cells, neither HOXB13ko alone nor HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 lines significantly differed from control cells, while LV-MEIS1 (with HOXB13 present) remained growth-suppressed (p<0.05, Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: In LAPC4 cells, deletion of HOXB13 significantly decreased proliferation to approximately the same rate as the LV-MEIS1 line compared to controls.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, in LAPC4 cells, deletion of HOXB13 significantly decreased proliferation to approximately the same rate as the LV-MEIS1 line compared to controls (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Loss of HOXB13 in LAPC4 cells was not associated with increased cell death.
source: Further analyses demonstrated that loss of HOXB13 in LAPC4 cells was not associated with increased cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Ectopic expression of LV-MEIS1 in LAPC4-HOXB13ko cells significantly increased proliferation compared to HOXB13ko.
source: However, in keeping with a requirement for HOXB13 expression with MEIS1 to enact a tumor suppressive effect, ectopic expression of LV-MEIS1 in LAPC4-HOXB13ko cells significantly increased proliferation compared to HOXB13ko (p<0.05 vs. HOXB13ko, Figure 3C), rather than further decreasing proliferation or remaining growth suppressed when HOXB13 was present.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: In both CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cells, HOXB13ko and HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 lines demonstrated significantly greater migration than LV-MEIS1 cells.
source: In both CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cells, HOXB13ko and HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 lines demonstrated significantly greater migration than LV-MEIS1 cells, while LV-MEIS1 continued to show significantly reduced migration compared to controls (p<0.05, Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 3D,E with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: LV-MEIS1 cells continued to show significantly reduced migration compared to controls.
source: In both CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cells, HOXB13ko and HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 lines demonstrated significantly greater migration than LV-MEIS1 cells, while LV-MEIS1 continued to show significantly reduced migration compared to controls (p<0.05, Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 3D,E with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: MEIS-mediated suppression of cell proliferation and migration in prostate cancer cells requires HOXB13 expression.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that MEIS-mediated suppression of cell proliferation and migration in PrCa cells requires HOXB13 expression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results with HOXB13 knockout cells

claim: Overall survival post-injection was significantly increased in LV-MEIS1 cells compared to control cells in an intracardiac injection metastasis model.
source: Overall survival post-injection was significantly increased in LV-MEIS1 cells compared to control cells naturally lacking detectable MEIS1 expression (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in overall survival between Control vs. HOXB13ko and HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 cells in an intracardiac injection metastasis model.
source: Further, in accordance with our in vitro data, there was no statistically significant difference in overall survival between Control vs. HOXB13ko and HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: LV-MEIS1 cells were the only condition in which bone metastases were not observed in an intracardiac injection metastasis model.
source: Notably, LV-MEIS1 cells were the only condition in which bone metastases were not observed.
evidence: Observation from in vivo metastasis study shown in Figure 4D

claim: MEIS1 suppresses prostate tumor growth and metastatic colonization in vivo.
source: These data demonstrate that MEIS1 suppresses prostate tumor growth and metastatic colonization in vivo, and the tumor-suppressive capability of MEIS1 in vivo is dependent upon expression and interaction with HOXB13.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from intracardiac injection metastasis model results

claim: The tumor-suppressive capability of MEIS1 in vivo is dependent upon expression and interaction with HOXB13.
source: These data demonstrate that MEIS1 suppresses prostate tumor growth and metastatic colonization in vivo, and the tumor-suppressive capability of MEIS1 in vivo is dependent upon expression and interaction with HOXB13.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from intracardiac injection metastasis model results comparing MEIS1 effects with and without HOXB13

claim: In the LV-MEIS1 line where both MEIS1 and HOXB13 are present, 7559 peaks were observed that were annotated to 4161 unique gene targets in MEIS1 ChIP-seq.
source: In the LV-MEIS1 line, where both MEIS1 and HOXB13 are present, we observed 7559 peaks that were annotated to 4161 unique gene targets (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1

claim: In the HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 line where MEIS1 is present but HOXB13 is absent, only 2048 peaks were observed that were annotated to 1617 unique gene targets in MEIS1 ChIP-seq.
source: In the HOXB13ko-LV-MEIS1 line, where MEIS1 is present but HOXB13 is absent, we observed only 2048 peaks that were annotated to 1617 unique gene targets (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2

claim: The reduction in the number of peaks and shift toward new peak locations of the MEIS1 cistrome in the absence of HOXB13 is supported by literature describing that HOX proteins stabilize MEIS1 on DNA.
source: The reduction in the number of peaks as well as the shift toward new peak locations of the MEIS1 cistrome in the absence of HOXB13 (Figure 5A) are supported by previous literature describing that HOX proteins stabilize MEIS1 on the DNA and that heterodimers of HOX and MEIS proteins develop latent motif specificity that is not demonstrated by either protein individually (Slattery et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of ChIP-seq data supported by citation to Slattery et al., 2011

claim: When both MEIS1 and HOXB13 were present, the HOXB13 motif was significantly conserved in MEIS1 peaks at a distance of 1 bp from the MEIS1 motif.
source: Unsurprisingly, when both MEIS1 and HOXB13 were present in the LV-MEIS1 line, the HOXB13 motif was significantly conserved in MEIS1 peaks at a distance of 1 bp from the MEIS1 motif itself, strongly supporting a direct interaction between these two proteins (p=2.84×10−12, Figure 5B top).
evidence: Supported by SpaMo analysis shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance p=2.84×10−12

claim: When HOXB13 was absent, the only HOX motif associated with MEIS1 was HOXA9, which is conserved at a distance of 3 bp from the MEIS1 motif.
source: On the other hand, when HOXB13 was absent, the only HOX motif associated with MEIS1 was HOXA9, which is conserved at a distance of 3 bp from the MEIS1 motif (p=1.14×10−6, Figure 5B bottom).
evidence: Supported by SpaMo analysis shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance p=1.14×10−6

claim: Integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data revealed 745 differentially expressed genes in CWR22Rv1-LV-MEIS1 compared to controls.
source: Integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data revealed 745 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (edgeR, fold-change >1.5 and FDR < 0.05) in CWR22Rv1-LV-MEIS1 compared to controls (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis with specified statistical thresholds

claim: Of 745 differentially expressed genes, 186 were directly targeted by MEIS1.
source: Of those 745 DEGs, 186 were directly targeted by MEIS1; of these targets, 29 genes were also bound by MEIS1 in the HOXB13ko condition and were thus removed since they would not be expected to be critical mediators of MEIS1–HOXB13-mediated tumor suppression.
evidence: Supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data

claim: 157 differentially expressed genes represent genes that are direct targets of MEIS1 only when HOXB13 is present.
source: The resulting 157 DEGs (Supplementary file 5) represent genes that are direct targets of MEIS1 only when HOXB13 is present and therefore represent prioritized candidates to elucidate the mechanism of MEIS1-dependent tumor suppression (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Proteoglycans in cancer was the most enriched pathway associated with MEIS1 and HOXB13 expression.
source: Pathway analyses of these 157 genes prioritized multiple putative pathways, of which 'proteoglycans in cancer' was the most enriched pathway associated with MEIS1 and HOXB13 expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: The majority of proteoglycans targeted by MEIS1 were upregulated by MEIS1 expression.
source: Further analyses documented that the majority of proteoglycans targeted by MEIS1 were upregulated by MEIS1 expression (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by volcano plot analysis shown in Figure 5E

claim: DCN was one of the most increased of the significant differentially expressed genes with fold-change of 11.38 and FDR of 7.37×10−12.
source: Of particular interest was elevated expression of DCN, which was one of the most increased of the significant DEGs in the dataset (fold-change = 11.38, FDR = 7.37×10−12).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis

claim: DCN belongs to the small-leucine-rich-proteoglycan family of proteins that has been well-documented to decrease tumor growth and progression.
source: DCN belongs to the small-leucine-rich-proteoglycan (SLRP) family of proteins that has been well-documented to decrease tumor growth and progression (Bi and Yang, 2013; Csordás et al., 2000; Edwards, 2012; Goldoni et al., 2009; Hildebrand et al., 1994; Iozzo et al., 1999; Järvinen and Prince, 2015; Khan et al., 2011; Santra et al., 2002; Schönherr et al., 1998; Schönherr et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Lumican increased with LV-MEIS1 expression with fold-change of 2.88 and FDR of 1.79×10−9.
source: Lumican (LUM), which also increased with LV-MEIS1 expression (fold-change = 2.88, FDR = 1.79×10−9), is another member of the tumor-suppressive SLRP protein family and has been shown to increase integrin B1 (ITGB1)-mediated adhesion as well as regulate expression of ITGB1 (D'Onofrio et al., 2008; Jeanne et al., 2017; Zeltz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis

claim: Lumican is a member of the tumor-suppressive SLRP protein family and has been shown to increase integrin B1-mediated adhesion and regulate expression of ITGB1.
source: Lumican (LUM), which also increased with LV-MEIS1 expression (fold-change = 2.88, FDR = 1.79×10−9), is another member of the tumor-suppressive SLRP protein family and has been shown to increase integrin B1 (ITGB1)-mediated adhesion as well as regulate expression of ITGB1 (D'Onofrio et al., 2008; Jeanne et al., 2017; Zeltz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to D'Onofrio et al., 2008; Jeanne et al., 2017; Zeltz et al., 2010

claim: TGFBR3 significantly increased with MEIS1 expression with fold-change of 1.67 and FDR of 4.13×10−4.
source: In parallel, TGFBR3 (also known as betaglycan) significantly increased with MEIS1 expression (fold-change = 1.67, FDR = 4.13×10−4) and has been shown to inhibit TGFβ signaling and decrease prostate tumor growth and progression in a manner similar to DCN (Ajiboye et al., 2010; Eickelberg et al., 2002; Sharifi et al., 2007; Turley et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis

claim: TGFBR3 has been shown to inhibit TGFβ signaling and decrease prostate tumor growth and progression in a manner similar to DCN.
source: In parallel, TGFBR3 (also known as betaglycan) significantly increased with MEIS1 expression (fold-change = 1.67, FDR = 4.13×10−4) and has been shown to inhibit TGFβ signaling and decrease prostate tumor growth and progression in a manner similar to DCN (Ajiboye et al., 2010; Eickelberg et al., 2002; Sharifi et al., 2007; Turley et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ajiboye et al., 2010; Eickelberg et al., 2002; Sharifi et al., 2007; Turley et al., 2007

claim: MEIS1 ChIP-Seq demonstrated binding in the DCN, LUM, and TGFBR3 genomic regions.
source: Analyses of MEIS1 ChIP-Seq demonstrated binding in the DCN, LUM, and TGFBR1 genomic region (Figure 5F), and independent ChIP-qPCR validated MEIS1 binding (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5F and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5G

claim: MEIS1 binding was significantly diminished when HOXB13 was deleted.
source: Importantly, MEIS1 binding was significantly diminished when HOXB13 was deleted (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F and G

claim: Increased mRNA expression of DCN, TGFBR3, LUM, and ITGB1 were validated at the protein level in both CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cell lines.
source: Increased mRNA expression of DCN, TGFBR3, LUM, and ITGB1 were validated at the protein level in both CWR22Rv1 and LAPC4 cell lines (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5H

claim: Increased protein expression of DCN, TGFBR3, LUM, and ITGB1 was not observed when HOXB13 was absent.
source: Additionally, increased protein expression was not observed when HOXB13 was absent, thus verifying the dependency of HOXB13 interaction to regulate expression of these targets.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5H

claim: The observed MEIS-mediated increase in DCN mRNA and protein expression was also observed in VCAP prostate cancer cell line.
source: The observed MEIS-mediated increase in DCN mRNA and protein expression was also observed in a third prostate cancer cell line, VCAP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: DCN is a multi-RTK inhibitor.
source: DCN is a multi-RTK inhibitor and likely has the broadest functional impact of these proteoglycans on cancer-associated pathways and response to growth factors.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The most well-established role for DCN is as an inhibitor of TGFβ signaling.
source: The most well-established role for DCN is as an inhibitor of TGFβ signaling (Baghy et al., 2012; Harper et al., 1994; Yamaguchi et al., 1990; Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baghy et al., 2012; Harper et al., 1994; Yamaguchi et al., 1990; Zhu et al., 2007

claim: DCN inhibits EGFR signaling after transient activation, leading to increased p21 expression.
source: DCN inhibits EGFR signaling after transient activation, leading to increased p21 expression (Csordás et al., 2000; Hu et al., 2009; Moscatello et al., 1998; Santra et al., 1997; Seidler et al., 2006), and DCN binds and inhibits IGF1R and downstream AKT signaling in cancer cells (Iozzo et al., 2011; Morrione et al., 2013; Schönherr et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: DCN binds and inhibits IGF1R and downstream AKT signaling in cancer cells.
source: DCN inhibits EGFR signaling after transient activation, leading to increased p21 expression (Csordás et al., 2000; Hu et al., 2009; Moscatello et al., 1998; Santra et al., 1997; Seidler et al., 2006), and DCN binds and inhibits IGF1R and downstream AKT signaling in cancer cells (Iozzo et al., 2011; Morrione et al., 2013; Schönherr et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iozzo et al., 2011; Morrione et al., 2013; Schönherr et al., 2005

claim: DCN antagonizes the c-MET receptor, which can lead to decreased non-canonical β-catenin and decreased cMYC.
source: DCN also antagonizes the c-MET receptor, which can lead to decreased non-canonical β-catenin and decreased cMYC (by way of increased phospho-T58, which destabilizes cMYC and leads to degradation) (Goldoni et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldoni et al., 2009

claim: The LV-MEIS1 condition where DCN expression is high has significantly decreased pathway activation for TGFβ, EGFR, WNT, and MYC gene sets.
source: The results in Figure 5I indicate that the LV-MEIS1 condition, where DCN expression is high, has significantly decreased pathway activation for TGFβ, (FDR: 0.039), EGFR (FDR: 0.036), WNT (FDR: 0.057), and MYC (FDR: 0.045) gene sets.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5I with specified FDR values

claim: Knockdown of DCN partially abrogated the growth suppression by LV-MEIS1 in CWR22Rv1 cells.
source: In comparison with the decreased proliferation observed with LV-MEIS1 expression, knockdown of DCN partially abrogated the growth suppression by LV-MEIS1 in CWR22v1 cells (p<0.05) but did not have a significant effect in LAPC4 cells (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Knockdown of DCN did not have a significant effect on growth suppression by LV-MEIS1 in LAPC4 cells.
source: In comparison with the decreased proliferation observed with LV-MEIS1 expression, knockdown of DCN partially abrogated the growth suppression by LV-MEIS1 in CWR22v1 cells (p<0.05) but did not have a significant effect in LAPC4 cells (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: siRNA knockdown of DCN in both LV-MEIS1 lines was sufficient to partially restore migratory capacity.
source: However, siRNA knockdown of DCN in both LV-MEIS1 lines was sufficient to partially restore migratory capacity (p<0.05, Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 6D,E with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: The HOXB13G84E mutation is associated with an increased odds ratio for colorectal cancer, bladder cancer, and leukemia.
